narrative.honest_line: the heaviest pressure seems to sit in how much you carry emotionally, alongside feeling lonely and unsure about reaching out to anyone for support.
narrative.narrative: Ananya, your responses suggest the biggest weight right now is emotional, with feelings that are hard to shake off and a sense that something bad may be coming. It sounds like you may be feeling lonely even around others, finding new friendships hard to make, and worrying about being judged if you ask for help. You may also be tying academic success closely to who you are, which can make everything feel heavier. Leaning on caffeine, tobacco or alcohol to cope, and getting little daylight, may be part of how you get through the day. Your academics look steadier, which is a real strength to notice.
narrative.loop_note: ...and the more alone it feels, the harder everything becomes to shake off, so stepping outside for some daylight may be the easiest link to change first.

priority_pages.name: Emotional Load & Coping
priority_pages.theory: When stress builds without a release, your body stays switched on — so small things feel big and rest doesn't feel restful. You can't think your way out of a racing body; calming the body first lets the thoughts follow. Naming what you feel, even with one word, can lower its intensity.

activities.name: 4-7-8 breathing
steps: Breathe in through your nose for 4 counts.
Hold for 7 counts, then breathe out slowly through your mouth for 8 counts.
Do two rounds. Then name one thing you can see, hear and feel.
activities.when: When worry or tension starts to spiral

activities.name: 60-second check-in
steps: Rate your stress from 0 to 10.
Write one word for what you're feeling right now.
Notice it without fixing it. Patterns become clear within a week.
activities.when: Every day, especially busy ones

priority_pages.name: Social & Belonging
priority_pages.theory: Carrying stress alone — especially after a breakup, a loss or a conflict with someone close — makes everything heavier. Grief after a relationship ends is real and takes real time; it's not a weakness. You don't need a therapist for your first honest conversation; you need one person and one honest sentence.

activities.name: One honest sentence
steps: Pick one person you trust (friend, cousin, roommate). Not for advice — just to be heard.
Send one honest sentence: 'The week is a lot, and I've been keeping it to myself.'
That's it. You don't owe them a solution. You've just shared the weight.
activities.when: Any day you'd normally say 'I'm fine'

activities.name: Study next to someone
steps: Pick the library, a common room or a friend's desk instead of studying alone.
You don't need to talk — just work in the same space.
Take one short break together and ask how their week is going.
activities.when: When evenings feel lonely

priority_pages.name: Identity & Self-worth
priority_pages.theory: Comparison and self-criticism can feel like motivation, but they mostly drain the energy you need for the actual work. Your mind notices what is undone far more than what is done, so the picture you carry of yourself is skewed. Writing down what you did — every night — slowly corrects that picture.

activities.name: Three-things-I-did list
steps: Before bed, write three things you actually did today — however small.
Not what's undone. Only what you did.
Read last week's list on Sunday; notice the evidence.
activities.when: When you feel you're never doing enough

activities.name: Worry check on paper
steps: Write the self-critical thought exactly as it sounds in your head.
List the evidence for it and the evidence against it.
Write a fairer version of the thought — one you'd say to a friend.
activities.when: When comparison or self-doubt keeps looping

priority_pages.name: Sleep, Lifestyle & Digital Pressure
priority_pages.theory: Late screens and late study push sleep later, and short sleep makes focus, mood and motivation run on low battery. This isn't about discipline — it's about protecting the fuel. A fixed wake-up time and the phone away before bed are the two easiest levers to pull first.

steps: Charge your phone across the room (or outside it) 30 minutes before you want to sleep.
Use a cheap alarm clock, or set the phone's alarm with volume loud enough.
If you need something to do, read a printed page or listen to music lying down.

priority_pages.name: Distraction & Delay Management
priority_pages.theory: At your age, your brain is still learning to say 'not now' to distractions — especially from screens. That's normal, not weak. The trick isn't 'be stronger' — it's to make the distraction harder to reach and the task easier to pick up.

activities.name: Phone in another room
activities.time: 30 sec at the start of study
steps: Before you sit to study, put your phone in a different room.
Not face-down on the desk — out of sight AND out of arm's reach.
If you need to look at something, get up, go get it, come back. The small walk makes it less automatic.
activities.when: Every study session

activities.name: Three-breath pause
steps: When you feel the urge to switch tasks, pause.
Take 3 slow breaths — in for 4, out for 6.
Ask yourself: 'What was I working on?' Return to that one thing. The urge usually passes in a minute.
activities.when: When you feel the urge to switch to phone / game / something else

priority_pages.name: Getting Started
priority_pages.theory: Starting a task is the hardest part — for every student. It's not laziness, it's a real brain thing. What helps isn't willpower; it's making the first step so tiny your brain can't say no. A 2-minute start beats 2 hours of worrying about starting.

activities.name: The 2-minute rule
steps: Pick the task you've been avoiding most.
Tell yourself: 'Just 2 minutes. Even if I stop after, that counts.'
Start the first step — open the book, write the date, copy the first line. Most days, you'll want to keep going.
activities.when: For any task you're avoiding

activities.name: First-step list
steps: For each homework, write ONLY the first physical action ('open notebook, write Q1' — not 'do maths').
Keep the list on your table where you can see it.
When you sit down, read the first item and do that one thing. The rest follows.
activities.when: When your mind goes blank on 'where to begin'

priority_pages.name: Energy, Rest & Study Balance
priority_pages.theory: Your brain runs on sleep, food, water, daylight and rest. At 11-13 you need about 9-11 hours of sleep, and screens late at night push sleep later. When energy is low, focus is low — fixing the body basics is often the fastest way to fix attention.

activities.name: Phone across the room before sleep
steps: 30 minutes before bed, put your phone or tablet to charge outside your room or across the room.
No videos in bed.
Read, talk, or listen to calm music instead.
activities.when: Every night

activities.name: Breakfast before leaving home

Keep a water bottle in your bag and drink through the day.
Notice how class feels on breakfast days.
activities.when: Every school morning

priority_pages.name: Emotional Overload & Coping
priority_pages.theory: When stress builds without a release, your body stays switched on — so small things feel big and rest doesn't feel restful. You can't think your way out of a racing body; calming the body first lets the thoughts follow. Naming what you feel, even in one word, takes some of its power away.

activities.name: 60-second check-in
steps: Rate your stress from 0 to 10.
Write one word for what you're feeling right now.
Notice it without fixing it. Patterns become clear within a week.
activities.when: Every day, especially busy ones

activities.name: 4-7-8 breathing
steps: Breathe in through your nose for 4 counts.
Hold for 7 counts, then breathe out slowly through your mouth for 8 counts.
Do two rounds. Then name one thing you can see, hear and feel.
activities.when: When worry or tension starts to spiral

priority_pages.name: Sleep, Lifestyle & Digital Pressure
priority_pages.theory: Late screens and late study push sleep later, and short sleep makes focus, mood and motivation run on low battery. This isn't about discipline — it's about protecting the fuel. A fixed wake-up time and the phone away before bed are the two easiest levers to pull first.

activities.name: Fixed wake-up time
steps: Choose one wake-up time you can keep all 7 days (within 30 minutes).
Keep it on weekends too — this, more than bedtime, resets your body clock.
If you slept badly, still get up on time; nap no more than 20 minutes.
activities.when: When your sleep timing keeps drifting

activities.name: Phone across the room
steps: Charge your phone across the room (or outside it) 30 minutes before you want to sleep.
Use a cheap alarm clock, or set the phone's alarm with volume loud enough.
If you need something to do, read a printed page or listen to music lying down.
activities.when: Any night you want sleep back

priority_pages.name: Parental & Family Expectations
priority_pages.theory: When home starts to feel like a scoreboard, every result seems to carry your family's happiness too. Expectations usually come from love and worry, but unspoken they turn into pressure. One honest, planned conversation — and remembering you are more than a comparison — gives everyone something real to work with.

activities.name: A 15-minute call home
steps: Call someone at home at a time you're both free.
Share one real update — not just 'all fine'.
Ask them one question about their week too.
activities.when: When you miss home or feel far away

activities.name: The fairer-thought exercise
activities.time: 3 min, when the inner critic hits
steps: Write the harsh thought exactly as it sounds ('I'm the only one who isn't sorted').
Ask: what would I say to a friend who said this about themselves?
Write one fairer sentence that is still true — and read it once out loud.
activities.when: When comparison at home or online makes you feel smaller

priority_pages.name: Peer Pressure & Social Acceptance
priority_pages.theory: Peer dynamics at your age swing hard — someone you trusted goes quiet, a group reshapes, a joke lands wrong. The pull to fit in is biological; it isn't a weakness in you. What helps most is one safe friend and one trusted adult who takes you seriously when it feels heavy.

activities.name: Tell one trusted adult
steps: Pick one adult who takes you seriously — parent, aunt / uncle, class teacher, elder cousin.
Say one honest line: 'Something at school has been bothering me and I'd like to tell you.'
You don't need advice — ask them to just listen first.
activities.when: Any time a peer problem feels too big to hold

activities.name: The no-script line
steps: Decide on one simple sentence: 'Not today, maybe later.' / 'Not my thing.' / 'My parents would notice.'
You don't owe reasons — a short line said calmly works best.
Walk away afterwards. Rehearse it once with a trusted adult if it helps.
activities.when: For peer pressure to do something you don't want to

priority_pages.name: Academic Stress & Study Habits
priority_pages.theory: When tests and homework pile up at Grade 10, your brain can't tell where to start - so it keeps starting with nothing. The way out isn't more hours; it's making the first step tiny. A 10-minute start beats hours of worrying, and three visible tasks always beats a vague pile of 'everything'.

activities.name: The 10-minute start
steps: Pick the subject you've avoided most. Write the first step in one line ('open chapter 6, copy the aim').
Set a 10-min timer, phone in another room. Do only that step.
When the timer rings, you may stop. Most days you'll want to continue a bit more.
activities.when: For the subject you've been avoiding most

activities.name: Morning top-3
steps: Before any screen, write the 3 things that must be done today.
Everything else waits for today.
Tick them off through the day. Keep the list in sight.
activities.when: Any day with more than one deadline on your head

priority_pages.name: Parental & Family Context
priority_pages.theory: When home starts to feel like a report card, every mark seems to carry your parents' mood too. Expectations and comparisons usually come from love and worry, but left unspoken they turn into pressure you carry alone. A short, calm talk that isn't about marks gives everyone something real to work with.

activities.name: Ten-minute parent check-in (no marks talk)
steps: Pick a calm moment — a walk, tea, a car ride — not right after a test result.
Agree on one rule for these 10 minutes: no marks, no ranks, no comparisons.
Share one thing from your day that has nothing to do with studies, and ask about theirs.
activities.when: When home has started to feel like a scoreboard

activities.name: Telling a parent what you need
steps: Finish this line on paper first: 'What would really help me right now is…'
Say it to one parent: 'I'm not asking you to fix anything — I just need ___.'
Agree one small thing to try this week, and check in on Sunday.
activities.when: When you feel unheard or compared at home

priority_pages.name: Getting Started
priority_pages.theory: Starting a task is the hardest part — for every student. It's not laziness, it's a real brain thing. What helps isn't willpower; it's making the first step so tiny your brain can't say no. A 2-minute start beats 2 hours of worrying about starting.

activities.name: The 2-minute rule
steps: Pick the task you've been avoiding most.
Tell yourself: 'Just 2 minutes. Even if I stop after, that counts.'
Start the first step — open the book, write the date, copy the first line. Most days, you'll want to keep going.
activities.when: For any task you're avoiding

activities.name: First-step list
steps: For each homework, write ONLY the first physical action ('open notebook, write Q1' — not 'do maths').
Keep the list on your table where you can see it.
When you sit down, read the first item and do that one thing. The rest follows.
activities.when: When your mind goes blank on 'where to begin'

priority_pages.name: Planning & Organisation
priority_pages.theory: Your brain can only hold a few things at once, so a plan that lives only in your head keeps slipping. Writing it down — what, when, where — does the remembering for you. Time also feels shorter than it is at your age, so a clock and a short list are your best friends.

activities.name: Colour-code today's top 3
steps: Write today's 3 most important tasks.
Colour them: red = must do today, yellow = should do, green = nice to do.
Start with red. Tick each when done.
activities.when: When there's too much and you don't know what comes first

activities.name: One-page deadline map
steps: On one page, write every test, project and homework due in the next 2 weeks.
Put a coloured dot next to the closest ones.
Stick it near your study spot and look at it every Sunday.
activities.when: When dates keep surprising you

priority_pages.name: Emotional Readiness for Learning
priority_pages.theory: Your feelings and your focus are connected. When you feel nervous, angry or overwhelmed, the 'thinking' part of the brain goes quiet and the 'alarm' part gets loud. Calming your body first — a few slow breaths — lets the thinking part switch back on.

activities.name: 60-second check-in before homework
steps: Before you open your books, stop for 60 seconds.
Ask: 'How do I feel right now?' Give it one word — calm, tired, worried, cross.
If the word is heavy, take 3 slow breaths or tell an adult before you start.
activities.when: Before every homework session
